title: TCP Three-Way Handshake
misconceptions: Believing that the initial sequence numbers (ISNs) always start at zero.
Thinking that user application payload data is typically transmitted inside the initial SYN packet.
Assuming the handshake only verifies that the server exists rather than synchronizing parameters for reliable delivery.
Believing the server can start sending application data before receiving the final ACK segment from the client.

rubric.text: Explains that TCP is a connection-oriented protocol that requires setting up a stateful connection before exchanging application data.
States that the client initiates the connection by sending a SYN packet containing its Initial Sequence Number (ISN) to the server.
States that the server responds with a SYN-ACK packet, acknowledging the client's SYN and sending its own ISN.
States that the client completes the handshake by sending an ACK packet to acknowledge the server's SYN segment.
Explains that sequence and acknowledgment numbers are incremented by one during SYN/ACK flag exchanges to acknowledge control signals.
Explains that Initial Sequence Numbers (ISNs) are chosen pseudo-randomly for security reasons rather than fixed at zero.
Clarifies that the handshake establishes bidirectional state, enabling independent full-duplex data flow control and error tracking.
Mentions that TCP options (such as Maximum Segment Size or Window Scaling) are negotiated within the SYN and SYN-ACK header fields.
